question.question: When a node's log store holds no entries beyond its last snapshot index - as after a monotonic-store installSnapshot that cleared the log, or after a restart that restored a snapshot with no retained logs - does the periodic trigger r.shouldSnapshot() correctly conclude that no new snapshot is due, or does it compute a wrapped delta and report a snapshot as due?
question.importance: runSnapshots calls shouldSnapshot on every SnapshotInterval and takes a full FSM snapshot whenever it returns true. If the subtraction between the log store's last index and the snapshot index wraps, a node in this state reports a snapshot as due forever: every interval it re-persists a complete snapshot and re-runs compaction for no new data, which is unbounded redundant IO/CPU on exactly the nodes with a cleared or compacted log. It is a resource/behaviour defect rather than a consensus-safety one, and the harness's decision is what makes it observable.

a MonotonicLogStore deployment where installSnapshot clears the log, and a restart that restored a snapshot without retaining logs

NewRaft restoreSnapshot -> setLastSnapshot(S) with an empty or cleared log store -> shouldSnapshot at the next interval

question.question: After appendEntries truncates a conflicting log suffix and resets the latest configuration to the committed one, is the resulting follower configuration state consistent with the log prefix it retains? Specifically, can configurations.latest/latestIndex (and the atomically published r.latestConfiguration that backs Raft.GetConfiguration) end up naming a configuration index that is no longer present in the follower's log, or a configuration that is not the one the retained committed prefix establishes?
question.importance: If a follower resumes with a latest configuration inconsistent with its retained log, then Raft.GetConfiguration reports a configuration the follower cannot justify, and every later membership decision that reads configurations.latest - the inConfiguration/hasVote rejections in requestVote and requestPreVote, the voter count in quorumSize, and the voters counted by checkLeaderLease - is taken on that configuration. A voter-count or membership error can shift which server sets form a quorum, affecting election and commitment safety.
contexts: a follower whose log suffix conflicts with a new leader's entries at an index at or below the follower's latest configuration index, with an uncommitted configuration entry inside the truncated range
a follower whose committed configuration index lies inside the truncated range
event_paths: processRPC -> appendEntries: prevLogTerm matches, a later entry.Index has a different term -> logs.DeleteRange(entry.Index, lastLogIdx) -> setLatestConfiguration(configurations.committed, configurations.committedIndex)
appendEntries -> StoreLogs(newEntries) -> processConfigurationLogEntry for each new entry -> setLastLog(last.Index, last.Term)

supporting_behavior_ids.b-request-vote: The vote handler's candidate-in-configuration and voter checks consume the latest configuration that the truncation path mutates, so they carry the consequence of an inconsistent rollback.
supporting_behavior_ids.b-follower-heartbeat-timeout: The election-abort guard compares latestIndex with committedIndex and tests voter membership against the latest configuration, so an inconsistent latest value changes whether this follower even starts an election.

counterevidence: The reset runs only under the guard entry.Index <= configurations.latestIndex (raft.go 1529-1531), and on a follower configurations.committedIndex is never greater than configurations.latestIndex: setCommittedConfiguration is called either with configurations.latest/ configurations.latestIndex (raft.go 1571, 1588, 1592; api.go 663) or with the snapshot configuration and its own index (raft.go 1938), so committedIndex <= latestIndex holds on every assignment.

For a legal leader the first conflicting index entry.Index is strictly greater than the follower's committedIndex: the entries at indices <= committedIndex are committed cluster-wide, and a legal leader's log matches every committed entry (log matching / Leader Completeness), so it cannot carry a different term there. Therefore entry.Index > committedIndex whenever the truncation branch is reached under a legal leader.

Because DeleteRange removes exactly [entry.Index, lastLogIdx] (raft.go 1524-1528) and committedIndex < entry.Index, the reset target committedIndex lies inside the retained prefix, so the reset configuration and its index are backed by a retained entry. Any uncommitted configuration entry at latestIndex is inside the truncated range, since the guard gives entry.Index <= latestIndex; no uncommitted configuration survives that the reset could contradict.

The reset is published consistently: setLatestConfiguration writes configurations.latest/ latestIndex and the atomic r.latestConfiguration copy in one call (raft.go 2216-2222), there is no separate committed atomic (api.go 160), and the only off-main-thread reader getLatestConfiguration is called solely by Raft.GetConfiguration (api.go 900), which therefore reports the same reset value that the main-thread consumers (requestVote, requestPreVote, quorumSize, checkLeaderLease) use.
unknowns: Whether a conflicting suffix at or below the follower's committed configuration index is reachable at all remains open; the counterevidence excludes it only for legal senders, so a deliberately malformed or byzantine AppendEntries is the boundary at which the guard would need re-examination.
question.trigger_rationale: The suspicion came from a single read of the truncation branch whose guard compares entry.Index only with latestIndex. Reading the remaining assignment sites of configurations.committed and the follower's commit-advancement path shows the guard is not used alone: it is combined with the log-matching invariant that keeps a legal leader from conflicting at or below the follower's committed configuration index. That closes the premise without needing a target run.

question.question: After appendEntries has already truncated a conflicting log suffix and the following StoreLogs of the leader's replacement entries fails, does the follower leave its in-memory log watermark (lastLog/lastLogIdx, read back by getLastLog/getLastIndex) consistent with the log it now durably holds, or does it keep a stale watermark that still counts the truncated indices? If the watermark is stale, does the leader's own recovery (nextIndex derived from the follower's reported LastLog) still bring the follower back into sync, or does it produce a persistent divergence that only a restart repairs?
question.importance: getLastIndex feeds both the AppendEntriesResponse.LastLog the leader uses to lower nextIndex and the follower's own previous-log check. If the watermark still includes a deleted index, the leader clamps nextIndex to a value whose previous entry the follower no longer has, so every subsequent AppendEntries is rejected at the same point without ever surfacing the leader-side ErrLogNotFound that would trigger a snapshot; the follower stays a divergent voter while reporting log state it does not hold. A stronger sub-case, that a later commit advancement applies indices the follower no longer holds, is left as an explicit unknown rather than assumed.
contexts: a follower whose LogStore accepts DeleteRange of the conflicting suffix but rejects the following StoreLogs of the leader's replacement entries
the leader whose per-follower nextIndex is derived from that follower's reported AppendEntriesResponse.LastLog
event_paths: appendEntries: entry.Term != storeEntry.Term -> logs.DeleteRange(entry.Index, lastLogIdx) succeeds -> logs.StoreLogs(newEntries) fails -> return with r.lastLog unchanged and resp.Success=false
replicateTo: AppendEntries rejected -> nextIndex = max(min(nextIndex-1, resp.LastLog+1), 1), where resp.LastLog is the follower's stale getLastIndex()

supporting_behavior_ids.b-replicate-follower: The leader's replicateTo lowers nextIndex using resp.LastLog and only falls back to a snapshot on its own ErrLogNotFound, so it carries the recovery consequence of the follower's reported watermark.
supporting_behavior_ids.b-fsm-apply: processLogs later reads the log by index from the store; if a subsequent request ever advances the commit/apply index past the truncation point, this reader is the consumer that would touch the missing range.

A controlled single-process check injects the store error, drives a conflicting AppendEntries, and reads both r.getLastLog() and the store's LastIndex() to see whether the two still agree.

question.importance: The watermark is the follower's claim about which log entries it holds. If installSnapshot leaves a pre-install watermark above the installed snapshot, the follower reports a LastLog it no longer has: on a monotonic store the log was removed, so the previous-log check and the follower's own reads address indices that are gone; on the leader side, sendLatestSnapshot sets nextIndex to S+1 after the install, but the very next AppendEntriesResponse.LastLog again reports the stale larger index, driving nextIndex back up while the leader's own compacted log cannot serve entries below S+1. The observable consequence is a follower that keeps re-receiving snapshots or rejects at the same point rather than resuming replication, and stale lastLogTerm can also satisfy a previous-log comparison against an index whose entry was removed.

grounding.derivation: installSnapshot sets lastApplied (raft.go 1930-1931), lastSnapshot (1933-1934) and the latest/committed configuration, then calls removeOldLogs for a MonotonicLogStore or compactLogs(req.LastLogIndex) otherwise (1939-1947); no setLastLog call appears anywhere in the handler. getLastIndex returns max(lastLogIndex,lastSnapshotIndex) and getLastEntry returns lastLog if lastLogIndex >= lastSnapshotIndex (state.go 145-162), so a pre-install watermark above S survives. appendEntries builds AppendEntriesResponse.LastLog from getLastIndex and uses getLastEntry/GetLog for the previous-log check, and the leader's sendLatestSnapshot sets nextIndex to meta.Index+1 while replicateTo lowers it from resp.LastLog (replication.go 366-372, 258-263).

materials.text:
# Raft Apply

Apply is the primary operation provided by raft. A client calls `raft.Apply` to apply
a command to the FSM. A command will first be committed, i.e., durably stored on a
quorum of raft nodes. Then, the committed command is applied to fsm.

This sequence diagram shows the steps involved in a `raft.Apply` operation. Each box
across the top is a separate thread. The name in the box identifies the state of the peer
(leader or follower) and the thread (`<peer state>:<thread name>`). When there are
multiple copies of the thread, it is indicated with `(each peer)`.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
   autonumber
 
   participant client
   participant leadermain as leader:main
   participant leaderfsm as leader:fsm
   participant leaderreplicate as leader:replicate (each peer)
   participant followermain as follower:main (each peer)

scope.description: Follower-side truncation path of appendEntries (raft.go) when a conflict is detected at an index at or below configurations.latestIndex, and the configuration state visible afterwards.
assumptions: The StableStore, LogStore and transport are the injected implementations; the transport delivers AppendEntries to the main thread.
The conflicting AppendEntries is well formed (prevLogTerm matches at PrevLogEntry) so the truncation branch is reached.
excluded: Leader-side configuration append and the stability gate (b-config-change-append).
Snapshot install/restore re-derivation of configuration.
Whether a legal leader can ever send the conflicting suffix that reaches the strongest sub-case.

units.rationale: First Candidate on the accepted v1 map. It fixes one attributed follower-side responsibility over F-config: after appendEntries truncates a conflicting suffix it resets only the latest configuration to the committed one (raft.go 1516-1531), while the committed configuration, the atomically published latest copy, and the retained log prefix are left as they were. The claim states the required consistency relation; the binding locates the exact truncation site. No violation is asserted: the code path has no guard that relates the reset latest index to the retained log, and what a follower then reports to GetConfiguration, to a RequestVote membership test, or to a following configuration entry is what a later check must observe.

audit_question.question: After appendEntries truncates a conflicting log suffix and resets the latest configuration to the committed one, is the resulting follower configuration state consistent with the log prefix it retains? Specifically, can configurations.latest/latestIndex (and the atomically published r.latestConfiguration that backs Raft.GetConfiguration) end up naming a configuration index that is no longer present in the follower's log, or a configuration that is not the one the retained committed prefix establishes?
audit_question.importance: If a follower resumes with a latest configuration inconsistent with its retained log, then Raft.GetConfiguration reports a configuration the follower cannot justify, and every later membership decision that reads configurations.latest - the inConfiguration/hasVote rejections in requestVote and requestPreVote, the voter count in quorumSize, and the voters counted by checkLeaderLease - is taken on that configuration. A voter-count or membership error can shift which server sets form a quorum, affecting election and commitment safety.
contexts: a follower whose log suffix conflicts with a new leader's entries at an index at or below the follower's latest configuration index, with an uncommitted configuration entry inside the truncated range
a follower whose committed configuration index lies inside the truncated range
event_paths: processRPC -> appendEntries: prevLogTerm matches, a later entry.Index has a different term -> logs.DeleteRange(entry.Index, lastLogIdx) -> setLatestConfiguration(configurations.committed, configurations.committedIndex)
appendEntries -> StoreLogs(newEntries) -> processConfigurationLogEntry for each new entry -> setLastLog(last.Index, last.Term)

supporting_behavior_ids.b-request-vote: The vote handler's candidate-in-configuration and voter checks consume the latest configuration that the truncation path mutates, so they carry the consequence of an inconsistent rollback.
supporting_behavior_ids.b-follower-heartbeat-timeout: The election-abort guard compares latestIndex with committedIndex and tests voter membership against the latest configuration, so an inconsistent latest value changes whether this follower even starts an election.

unknowns: Whether a conflicting entry can legally appear at an index at or below the follower's latestIndex while the committed configuration index is strictly greater than entry.Index (i.e. whether the truncation can delete the entry backing the committed configuration) is not established from the library alone; it depends on the sending leader's log.

Whether the atomically published r.latestConfiguration is ever read by a consumer that acts before the main thread re-derives configuration state is not yet traced for every caller of getLatestConfiguration.
The behavior of a subsequent AppendEntries carrying no configuration entry after such a rollback was not traced for the case where latestIndex == committedIndex before truncation.
audit_question.trigger_rationale: A single read of the truncation branch (raft.go 1516-1531) shows a configuration reset whose guard compares entry.Index only with latestIndex and never with the retained log or the committed configuration index. That is a sourced difference between the mutation and the consistency its consumers need, and it is exercisable in a controlled single-process cluster by forcing a conflicting suffix that contains a configuration entry.

scope.description: The appendEntries error path after a successful truncation and a failing StoreLogs (raft.go 1524-1544), and the recovery it leaves for the leader's per-follower replication loop.
assumptions: The LogStore is the injected implementation; a DeleteRange may succeed while a following StoreLogs of other entries returns an error, and the error is a legal return of the LogStore interface.
The conflicting AppendEntries is well formed (prevLogTerm matches at PrevLogEntry) so the truncation branch is reached before the store write fails.
excluded: Required durability of a store that fails mid-batch; the check does not assert what a store must do, only how Raft continues.
Leader-side configuration and snapshot machinery beyond the ErrLogNotFound trigger in setupAppendEntries.
Any claim that the process panics.

units.rationale: Second Candidate, on the accepted v1 map. This is a fault-handling gap the code itself admits: appendEntries deletes the conflicting suffix (raft.go 1524-1533) and then, if StoreLogs of the replacement entries fails, returns leaving r.lastLog/lastLogIdx still describing the deleted indices (raft.go 1537-1544, with the author's own TODO). getLastIndex then reports the deleted index to the leader, whose nextIndex recovery consumes exactly that value.

audit_question.question: After appendEntries has already truncated a conflicting log suffix and the following StoreLogs of the leader's replacement entries fails, does the follower leave its in-memory log watermark (lastLog/lastLogIdx, read back by getLastLog/getLastIndex) consistent with the log it now durably holds, or does it keep a stale watermark that still counts the truncated indices? If the watermark is stale, does the leader's own recovery (nextIndex derived from the follower's reported LastLog) still bring the follower back into sync, or does it produce a persistent divergence that only a restart repairs?
audit_question.importance: getLastIndex feeds both the AppendEntriesResponse.LastLog the leader uses to lower nextIndex and the follower's own previous-log check. If the watermark still includes a deleted index, the leader clamps nextIndex to a value whose previous entry the follower no longer has, so every subsequent AppendEntries is rejected at the same point without ever surfacing the leader-side ErrLogNotFound that would trigger a snapshot; the follower stays a divergent voter while reporting log state it does not hold. A stronger sub-case, that a later commit advancement applies indices the follower no longer holds, is left as an explicit unknown rather than assumed.
contexts: a follower whose LogStore accepts DeleteRange of the conflicting suffix but rejects the following StoreLogs of the leader's replacement entries
the leader whose per-follower nextIndex is derived from that follower's reported AppendEntriesResponse.LastLog
event_paths: appendEntries: entry.Term != storeEntry.Term -> logs.DeleteRange(entry.Index, lastLogIdx) succeeds -> logs.StoreLogs(newEntries) fails -> return with r.lastLog unchanged and resp.Success=false
replicateTo: AppendEntries rejected -> nextIndex = max(min(nextIndex-1, resp.LastLog+1), 1), where resp.LastLog is the follower's stale getLastIndex()

supporting_behavior_ids.b-replicate-follower: The leader's replicateTo lowers nextIndex using resp.LastLog and only falls back to a snapshot on its own ErrLogNotFound, so it carries the recovery consequence of the follower's reported watermark.
supporting_behavior_ids.b-fsm-apply: processLogs later reads the log by index from the store; if a subsequent request ever advances the commit/apply index past the truncation point, this reader is the consumer that would touch the missing range.

unknowns: Whether a later AppendEntries can advance the follower's commit index past the truncation point while the watermark is stale, which would make processLogs read an index the store no longer holds, was not established; the reachable consequence may be limited to the persistent rejection loop.

Whether any store implementation in the snapshot is expected to make StoreLogs succeed after a successful DeleteRange (e.g. an atomic batch) is not established; the failure is treated as a legal error return of the injected LogStore.
Whether a restart or a snapshot install is the only repair, and whether any in-library path recomputes lastLog from the store without a restart, was not traced.
audit_question.trigger_rationale: The failure scenario is concrete and local: one injected LogStore error after the library has already mutated the durable log. The follower's own comment names the resulting wrong state, and the leader's nextIndex formula consumes the very value that is left stale, so the effect is not confined to the follower. A controlled single-process check injects the store error, drives a conflicting AppendEntries, and reads both r.getLastLog() and the store's LastIndex() to see whether the two still agree.

scope.description: The installSnapshot success path (raft.go 1814-1955) after the snapshot is restored, in particular the absence of any setLastLog before the log store is cleared or compacted, and the readers of the resulting watermark.
assumptions: The SnapshotStore and LogStore are the injected implementations; the snapshot restore and the log clear/compaction are the unmodified library calls.
The follower's in-memory watermark index can be greater than the installed snapshot's LastLogIndex when the install begins.
excluded: Required durability of the injected stores.
Any change to the RPC framing or snapshot streaming path.
The correctness of the leader's snapshot contents.

units.rationale: Third Candidate, on the accepted v1 map, opened after the store-failure lead was confirmed. Reading installSnapshot end to end shows that the handler updates lastApplied, the snapshot index/term and the configuration, and then clears or compacts the log store, but never updates the in-memory log watermark through setLastLog (raft.go 1814-1955; the tail calls setLastApplied/setLastSnapshot and then removeOldLogs or compactLogs). getLastIndex/getLastEntry take the maximum of that watermark and the snapshot index (state.go 145-162), so a follower whose previous watermark index exceeds the installed snapshot index keeps reporting the old, larger index - and on a monotonic store the log it referred to has just been removed. The claim states the required post-install consistency; the binding locates the install handler.

audit_question.question: After installSnapshot accepts a snapshot at index S and then clears (MonotonicLogStore) or compacts (otherwise) the log store, does the follower leave its in-memory log watermark (lastLogIndex/lastLogTerm as read by getLastLog/getLastIndex/getLastEntry) consistent with the durable state it now holds, or can it keep the pre-install watermark when that index is greater than S? If it keeps the old watermark, what do the consumers of that value - the follower's own previous-log check in appendEntries, the AppendEntriesResponse.LastLog the leader uses to set nextIndex, and the leader's post-snapshot nextIndex = meta.Index+1 - then describe?
audit_question.importance: The watermark is the follower's claim about which log entries it holds. If installSnapshot leaves a pre-install watermark above the installed snapshot, the follower reports a LastLog it no longer has: on a monotonic store the log was removed, so the previous-log check and the follower's own reads address indices that are gone; on the leader side, sendLatestSnapshot sets nextIndex to S+1 after the install, but the very next AppendEntriesResponse.LastLog again reports the stale larger index, driving nextIndex back up while the leader's own compacted log cannot serve entries below S+1. The observable consequence is a follower that keeps re-receiving snapshots or rejects at the same point rather than resuming replication, and stale lastLogTerm can also satisfy a previous-log comparison against an index whose entry was removed.
contexts: a follower that accepts an InstallSnapshot whose LastLogIndex is smaller than the follower's current in-memory log watermark index
a MonotonicLogStore follower whose log is cleared by removeOldLogs during the install
event_paths: installSnapshot: snapshot restored -> setLastApplied(S) -> setLastSnapshot(S,term) -> configurations replaced -> removeOldLogs()/compactLogs(S) -> resp.Success=true (no setLastLog)
appendEntries after the install: a.PrevLogEntry compared against getLastEntry()/GetLog, and resp.LastLog = getLastIndex() = max(lastLogIndex, S)

supporting_behavior_ids.b-append-entries: appendEntries is the consumer that reads the watermark for the previous-log check and for the AppendEntriesResponse.LastLog it returns, so it carries the consequence of a stale post-install watermark.
supporting_behavior_ids.b-replicate-follower: The leader's sendLatestSnapshot sets nextIndex to meta.Index+1 and replicateTo's rejection path lowers it from response.LastLog, so the leader-side recovery effect of the stale watermark is carried here.

unknowns: Whether a follower whose watermark exceeds the leader's snapshot index is reachable in a legal history, and how often, was not established: it needs a follower with a longer uncommitted tail than the leader's compacted snapshot, which depends on the sending leader's log and compaction timing.

Whether the leader's next AppendEntries after a successful install actually re-raises nextIndex from the stale response value, or whether the follower's log is already consistent enough to accept, was not traced.

Whether compactLogs(S) with the default TrailingLogs can leave the follower's old entries above S in place, so that the stale watermark still names an entry the store happens to hold, was not traced for the non-monotonic default.
audit_question.trigger_rationale: The gap is local and readable: installSnapshot is the only handler that replaces the durable log prefix wholesale and the only one that never calls setLastLog, while both the follower's own readers and the leader's recovery consume that value. A controlled single-process check can seed a follower whose watermark is above the snapshot index, drive InstallSnapshot, and read getLastLog/getLastIndex against the snapshot index and the store, which distinguishes a reset watermark from a stale one.

selections.rationale: Recover core understanding of the HashiCorp raft (Go) implementation: describe the formation/advancement line and the authority/term-context line from read source, and explain how the two connect. The map name cites the actual owner/handlers observed in raft.go, commitment.go, fsm.go, replication.go, api.go and snapshot.go; both core paths are grounded and the connection is the term fence on entries plus the startIndex commitment restriction and the ErrLeadershipLost sweep on step-down.

feedback.answered: The initial two-line question is answered for this implementation: decisions form as (index,term) log entries replicated by per-peer goroutines, and advance only when commitment.recalculate finds a quorum voter match at or beyond the leader's term startIndex; authority is a durable per-instance term plus at most one persisted vote, and context is adopted from any higher-term RPC. The connection is the term on every entry, the startIndex commitment restriction on prior-term entries, the ErrLeadershipLost answer to pending futures on step-down, and the rollback of an uncommitted configuration when a follower truncates a conflicting suffix.
remaining: No defect is asserted yet; the map records where pending support and authority interact but does not evaluate whether any interaction is unsafe.

One sourced lead worth a bounded investigation: in appendEntries a conflict at an index at or below configurations.latestIndex resets only the latest configuration to the committed one, while the committed configuration and the commitment object are untouched; what a follower in that state advertises to a subsequent RequestVote or what a subsequent AppendEntries with a configuration entry does was not traced.

Client-contract completion (A7): a future enqueued on applyCh that is never committed relies on a caller-supplied timeout; whether the library itself owes any completion for an admitted-but-uncommitted command was not established.
feedback.rationale: Semantic facts are kept distinct from normative claims and from execution evidence. The map cites only read source ranges; unread paths (pipeline internals, leadership-transfer interaction, external snapshot restore) are recorded as core_overview.open_details, and no obligation is asserted.

after.purpose: Form a decision (leader election / log agreement) and advance the replicated log legally.
after.realization_summary: The leader main thread appends entries to its LogStore, dispatches them onto inflight futures, and a per-peer replication goroutine copies entries to followers via AppendEntries; the commitment object aggregates per-voter durable match indexes and advances the leader commit index once a quorum matches at or beyond the term's startIndex, after which the leader hands committed entries to the FSM goroutine.

after.purpose: Acquire, transfer or lose authority and keep the term/leader context valid.
after.realization_summary: A follower that times out starts a candidate loop; a campaign (optionally pre-vote) raises currentTerm, persists a self-vote and tallies RequestVote responses up to a majority. Followers adopt a leader identity and raise their term on AppendEntries/RequestVote/InstallSnapshot, and a leader steps down on a newer term or when its lease quorum lapses.

after.purpose: Recover and resynchronize an eligible participant that has fallen behind the log.
after.realization_summary: An InstallSnapshot RPC lets a leader ship a full snapshot to a lagging follower, which spills it to a local SnapshotStore, restores the FSM, moves lastApplied/lastSnapshot and adopts the snapshot's configuration. At startup an instance restores the newest usable local snapshot before scanning configuration entries.

after.purpose: Maintain configuration and participant eligibility as an authoritative replicated decision.
after.realization_summary: AddVoter/AddNonvoter/RemoveServer/DemoteVoter enqueue a configurationChangeRequest that the leader turns into a single configuration log entry (or a legacy peer entry for protocol < 2); the entry is committed like any other and, once committed, the committed configuration changes voter eligibility. Latest and committed configuration indexes are tracked separately.

after.purpose: Apply committed decisions to the caller FSM and report completion.
after.realization_summary: The FSM goroutine receives batches of commitTuple on fsmMutateCh and calls FSM.Apply (or ApplyBatch), or ingests a restored snapshot; it responds to the associated logFuture with the FSM result and tracks lastIndex/lastTerm.

after.purpose: Persist and reconstruct the history that supports decisions.
after.realization_summary: Term, last vote, log entries, configuration indexes and snapshots are written to caller-supplied durable stores; setCurrentTerm persists before updating memory, persistence of a vote is a precondition of granting it, and log compaction/snapshots bound log growth.

after.purpose: Expose the invocation interval and observed completion of client operations.
after.realization_summary: Client calls enqueue a logFuture/verifyFuture on a channel; the returned Future is completed when the leader applies the entry, when leadership is lost (ErrLeadershipLost), or on timeout/shutdown. The library owns the future contract; the caller owns when to call and how to interpret results.

after.meaning: The highest log index this instance treats as committed: on a leader, a quorum durable match at or beyond the term's startIndex; on a follower, min(LeaderCommitIndex, lastIndex).
after.validity_context: monotonic within an instance; a follower's value is derived from the current leader's advertised LeaderCommitIndex.
after.durability: not itself persisted; recomputed from the log and configuration, but bounded by startIndex while a leader.
after.recovery: after restart the commit index is re-derived as entries are re-applied or re-advertised by a leader.

after.meaning: The cluster configuration (servers, suffrage) as latest and as committed, each with the log index of its configuration entry.

identity.component: latest and committed Configuration with their indexes

after.validity_context: latest configuration may be uncommitted; committed configuration is the one whose entry is committed and is what determines current voter eligibility.
after.durability: encoded in configuration log entries and in snapshot metadata.
after.recovery: NewRaft scans log entries after the last snapshot to rebuild the latest/committed configuration.

after.meaning: The monotonic term this instance currently believes it is in; used as the fence for every vote, entry acceptance and authority decision.
after.validity_context: valid from the moment the durable write succeeds until replaced by a strictly greater term; survives restart because it is read back in NewRaft.
after.durability: written to the caller StableStore before the in-memory value changes.
after.recovery: NewRaft reads CurrentTerm from StableStore at start.

after.meaning: The highest log index the caller FSM has ingested, either through Apply/ApplyBatch or through a Restore of a snapshot.
after.validity_context: advances only after the FSM has consumed the entry; used to decide what to replay after restart.
after.durability: held by the caller FSM; the Raft library only remembers lastSnapshot durably.
after.recovery: on start, the snapshot index becomes lastApplied and later log entries are re-applied.

after.meaning: The leader address and ID this instance currently attributes authority to, advertised to clients and used to reject conflicting vote requests.
after.validity_context: cleared on every state transition and re-established when a claiming leader's RPC is accepted.
after.durability: not durable; reconstructed after restart from the first accepted RPC from a leader.
after.recovery: unknown after restart until a leader contacts the instance.

after.meaning: A replicated log entry identified by (index, term, type, data) that carries client commands, barriers, no-ops and configuration changes.
after.validity_context: valid as written; a leader may overwrite a follower's suffix at the same index with a different term during conflict resolution.
after.durability: leader and follower both call LogStore.StoreLogs; conflicting suffixes are deleted with DeleteRange.
after.recovery: lastIndex/lastLog are read from LogStore in NewRaft and replayed from the last snapshot.

after.meaning: The single candidate this instance has voted for within the current term, the safety record that prevents a second vote in the same term after a restart.
after.validity_context: valid for the term recorded alongside it; replaced when a later term is voted in.
after.durability: persistVote writes both keys; a grant is only answered after a successful persist.
after.recovery: Read back by requestVote on subsequent requests.

after.meaning: A durable snapshot of the FSM at a given index/term together with the configuration in force at that index.
after.validity_context: valid once Persist has committed it and it is listed by the SnapshotStore; older snapshots may be removed.
after.durability: written by the SnapshotStore implementation; the library tracks only the index/term of the newest snapshot.
after.recovery: restoreSnapshot at startup and installSnapshot at runtime both rebuild state from it.

formation.explanation: A decision is formed as a log entry and advanced only after a quorum has durably stored it. The leader's dispatchLogs assigns (index, term) to each logFuture, stores it locally and records its own match; each peer's followerReplication goroutine copies entries with AppendEntries and, on success, records that peer's durable match index through commitment.match. commitment.recalculate sorts the voter match indexes, takes the quorum-position match and advances commitIndex only when it is both above the current value and at or beyond the term's startIndex. leaderLoop consumes commitCh, moves the inflight prefix up to the commit index and hands it to the FSM goroutine. A follower mirrors this by clamping its commit index to min(LeaderCommitIndex, lastIndex) and applying the same logs.

context.explanation: Authority is a per-instance, durable term plus at most one vote. A follower that stops hearing from a leader starts a candidate loop that raises currentTerm (persisted first) and solicits votes, optionally behind a non-mutating pre-vote. A vote is granted only to a candidate in the configuration whose log is at least as up to date, and only after the vote is persisted, so the same term cannot vote twice even across restart. Any RPC carrying a higher term forces the receiver to Follower and adopts the sender's term and, for leader RPCs, the sender's leader identity. A leader keeps authority while a quorum of voters is in recent contact and abandons it on a newer term, a failed verification, or a lapsed lease.

connection.explanation: The two core lines meet at the term fence carried by every entry. A log entry is only meaningful together with the term of the leader that wrote it: a follower accepts new entries only when the previous-log coordinate matches its own log and only after adopting a term that is not older, and a new leader may not commit an entry from an earlier term merely because it is stored on a majority — commitment.startIndex forces the current term's opening no-op (or an equivalent entry) to be committed first. Conversely, authority transitions constrain which pending support may still be consumed: when a leader steps down it answers every inflight logFuture and pending verifyFuture with ErrLeadershipLost, and a follower that truncates a conflicting suffix also rolls its latest configuration back to the committed one, so an uncommitted configuration cannot survive on a minority that lost the election.

question.question: After appendEntries truncates a conflicting log suffix and resets the latest configuration to the committed one, is the resulting follower configuration state consistent with the log prefix it retains? Specifically, can configurations.latest/latestIndex (and the atomically published r.latestConfiguration that backs Raft.GetConfiguration) end up naming a configuration index that is no longer present in the follower's log, or a configuration that is not the one the retained committed prefix establishes?
question.importance: If a follower resumes with a latest configuration inconsistent with its retained log, then Raft.GetConfiguration reports a configuration the follower cannot justify, and every later membership decision that reads configurations.latest - the inConfiguration/hasVote rejections in requestVote and requestPreVote, the voter count in quorumSize, and the voters counted by checkLeaderLease - is taken on that configuration. A voter-count or membership error can shift which server sets form a quorum, affecting election and commitment safety.

For a legal leader the first conflicting index entry.Index is strictly greater than the follower's committedIndex: the entries at indices <= committedIndex are committed cluster-wide, and a legal leader's log matches every committed entry (log matching / Leader Completeness), so it cannot carry a different term there. Because DeleteRange removes exactly [entry.Index, lastLogIdx] (raft.go 1524-1528) and committedIndex < entry.Index, the reset target committedIndex lies inside the retained prefix, so the reset configuration and its index are backed by a retained entry. Any uncommitted configuration entry at latestIndex is inside the truncated range, since the guard gives entry.Index <= latestIndex; no uncommitted configuration survives that the reset could contradict.

Apply is the primary operation provided by raft. A client calls `raft.Apply` to apply
a command to the FSM. A command will first be committed, i.e., durably stored on a
quorum of raft nodes. Then, the committed command is applied to fsm.

across the top is a separate thread. The name in the box identifies the state of the peer
(leader or follower) and the thread (`<peer state>:<thread name>`). When there are
multiple copies of the thread, it is indicated with `(each peer)`.

audit_question.question: After appendEntries has already truncated a conflicting log suffix and the following StoreLogs of the leader's replacement entries fails, does the follower leave its in-memory log watermark (lastLog/lastLogIdx, read back by getLastLog/getLastIndex) consistent with the log it now durably holds, or does it keep a stale watermark that still counts the truncated indices? If the watermark is stale, does the leader's own recovery (nextIndex derived from the follower's reported LastLog) still bring the follower back into sync, or does it produce a persistent divergence that only a restart repairs?
audit_question.importance: getLastIndex feeds both the AppendEntriesResponse.LastLog the leader uses to lower nextIndex and the follower's own previous-log check. If the watermark still includes a deleted index, the leader clamps nextIndex to a value whose previous entry the follower no longer has, so every subsequent AppendEntries is rejected at the same point without ever surfacing the leader-side ErrLogNotFound that would trigger a snapshot; the follower stays a divergent voter while reporting log state it does not hold. A stronger sub-case, that a later commit advancement applies indices the follower no longer holds, is left as an explicit unknown rather than assumed.

the leader whose per-follower nextIndex is derived from that follower's reported AppendEntriesResponse.LastLog

replicateTo: AppendEntries rejected -> nextIndex = max(min(nextIndex-1, resp.LastLog+1), 1), where resp.LastLog is the follower's stale getLastIndex()

supporting_behavior_ids.b-replicate-follower: The leader's replicateTo lowers nextIndex using resp.LastLog and only falls back to a snapshot on its own ErrLogNotFound, so it carries the recovery consequence of the follower's reported watermark.

audit_question.importance: The watermark is the follower's claim about which log entries it holds. If installSnapshot leaves a pre-install watermark above the installed snapshot, the follower reports a LastLog it no longer has: on a monotonic store the log was removed, so the previous-log check and the follower's own reads address indices that are gone; on the leader side, sendLatestSnapshot sets nextIndex to S+1 after the install, but the very next AppendEntriesResponse.LastLog again reports the stale larger index, driving nextIndex back up while the leader's own compacted log cannot serve entries below S+1. The observable consequence is a follower that keeps re-receiving snapshots or rejects at the same point rather than resuming replication, and stale lastLogTerm can also satisfy a previous-log comparison against an index whose entry was removed.

audit_question.importance: runSnapshots calls shouldSnapshot on every SnapshotInterval and takes a full FSM snapshot whenever it returns true. If the subtraction between the log store's last index and the snapshot index wraps, a node in this state reports a snapshot as due forever: every interval it re-persists a complete snapshot and re-runs compaction for no new data, which is unbounded redundant IO/CPU on exactly the nodes with a cleared or compacted log. It is a resource/behaviour defect rather than a consensus-safety one, and the harness's decision is what makes it observable.

selections.rationale: Recover core understanding of the HashiCorp raft (Go) implementation: describe the formation/advancement line and the authority/term-context line from read source, and explain how the two connect. The map name cites the actual owner/handlers observed in raft.go, commitment.go, fsm.go, replication.go, api.go and snapshot.go; both core paths are grounded and the connection is the term fence on entries plus the startIndex commitment restriction and the ErrLeadershipLost sweep on step-down.

feedback.answered: The initial two-line question is answered for this implementation: decisions form as (index,term) log entries replicated by per-peer goroutines, and advance only when commitment.recalculate finds a quorum voter match at or beyond the leader's term startIndex; authority is a durable per-instance term plus at most one persisted vote, and context is adopted from any higher-term RPC. The connection is the term on every entry, the startIndex commitment restriction on prior-term entries, the ErrLeadershipLost answer to pending futures on step-down, and the rollback of an uncommitted configuration when a follower truncates a conflicting suffix.
remaining: No defect is asserted yet; the map records where pending support and authority interact but does not evaluate whether any interaction is unsafe.

One sourced lead worth a bounded investigation: in appendEntries a conflict at an index at or below configurations.latestIndex resets only the latest configuration to the committed one, while the committed configuration and the commitment object are untouched; what a follower in that state advertises to a subsequent RequestVote or what a subsequent AppendEntries with a configuration entry does was not traced.

formation.explanation: A decision is formed as a log entry and advanced only after a quorum has durably stored it. The leader's dispatchLogs assigns (index, term) to each logFuture, stores it locally and records its own match; each peer's followerReplication goroutine copies entries with AppendEntries and, on success, records that peer's durable match index through commitment.match. commitment.recalculate sorts the voter match indexes, takes the quorum-position match and advances commitIndex only when it is both above the current value and at or beyond the term's startIndex. leaderLoop consumes commitCh, moves the inflight prefix up to the commit index and hands it to the FSM goroutine. A follower mirrors this by clamping its commit index to min(LeaderCommitIndex, lastIndex) and applying the same logs.

context.explanation: Authority is a per-instance, durable term plus at most one vote. A follower that stops hearing from a leader starts a candidate loop that raises currentTerm (persisted first) and solicits votes, optionally behind a non-mutating pre-vote. A vote is granted only to a candidate in the configuration whose log is at least as up to date, and only after the vote is persisted, so the same term cannot vote twice even across restart. Any RPC carrying a higher term forces the receiver to Follower and adopts the sender's term and, for leader RPCs, the sender's leader identity. A leader keeps authority while a quorum of voters is in recent contact and abandons it on a newer term, a failed verification, or a lapsed lease.

connection.explanation: The two core lines meet at the term fence carried by every entry. A log entry is only meaningful together with the term of the leader that wrote it: a follower accepts new entries only when the previous-log coordinate matches its own log and only after adopting a term that is not older, and a new leader may not commit an entry from an earlier term merely because it is stored on a majority — commitment.startIndex forces the current term's opening no-op (or an equivalent entry) to be committed first. Conversely, authority transitions constrain which pending support may still be consumed: when a leader steps down it answers every inflight logFuture and pending verifyFuture with ErrLeadershipLost, and a follower that truncates a conflicting suffix also rolls its latest configuration back to the committed one, so an uncommitted configuration cannot survive on a minority that lost the election.

selections.rationale: First Candidate on the accepted v1 map. It fixes one attributed follower-side responsibility over F-config: after appendEntries truncates a conflicting suffix it resets only the latest configuration to the committed one (raft.go 1516-1531), while the committed configuration, the atomically published latest copy, and the retained log prefix are left as they were. The claim states the required consistency relation; the binding locates the exact truncation site. No violation is asserted: the code path has no guard that relates the reset latest index to the retained log, and what a follower then reports to GetConfiguration, to a RequestVote membership test, or to a following configuration entry is what a later check must observe.

Source reading resolves the suspicion raised by the truncation branch: the reset latest := committed cannot name a configuration that is not backed by the follower's retained prefix, because the reset only runs when entry.Index <= latestIndex and, for any legal leader, the first conflicting index is strictly greater than the follower's committed configuration index. The mechanism is recorded as counterevidence and the two answered unknowns are removed through sourced feedback; the illegal-sender sub-case is kept as the independent remaining boundary. No execution is needed to dispose this premise, so no check is manufactured and no obligation is re-stated.

feedback.answered: The follower-side configuration rollback in appendEntries is consistent with the retained log for any legal history: the reset latest := committed at committedIndex only runs when entry.Index <= latestIndex, while a legal leader's first conflicting index is always greater than the follower's committedIndex, so the reset target is inside the retained prefix and every uncommitted configuration it could contradict was removed by the same truncation. The published and consumed latest value is updated in one write, so GetConfiguration and the membership/voter checks agree.
remaining: The illegal-sender boundary stays open: a malformed AppendEntries with a conflict at or below committedIndex would reach a state the guard does not cover; nothing in the library is claimed to defend against that.

Third Candidate, on the accepted v1 map, opened after the store-failure lead was confirmed. Reading installSnapshot end to end shows that the handler updates lastApplied, the snapshot index/term and the configuration, and then clears or compacts the log store, but never updates the in-memory log watermark through setLastLog (raft.go 1814-1955; the tail calls setLastApplied/setLastSnapshot and then removeOldLogs or compactLogs). getLastIndex/getLastEntry take the maximum of that watermark and the snapshot index (state.go 145-162), so a follower whose previous watermark index exceeds the installed snapshot index keeps reporting the old, larger index - and on a monotonic store the log it referred to has just been removed. The claim states the required post-install consistency; the binding locates the install handler.

after.meaning: The instance's in-memory claim of the last durable log coordinate it holds: lastLogIndex/lastLogTerm together with lastSnapshotIndex/lastSnapshotTerm, surfaced through getLastLog, getLastEntry and getLastIndex. It is the value a follower returns as AppendEntriesResponse.LastLog, the value it compares an incoming previous-log coordinate against, and the last-log coordinate a candidate advertises when soliciting votes.
after.validity_context: Valid only while it describes the log and snapshot the instance actually holds. Appending raises the log part; a conflict truncation replaces it; installSnapshot and snapshot compaction can remove the entries an older value named. It is not persisted: NewRaft derives the log part from LogStore.LastIndex and the snapshot part from the stable store, so a restart recomputes it from durable state. The two confirmed gaps recorded in this Fact's unknowns are both violations of this validity condition within the runtime transitions.
after.durability: In-memory only. A restart rebuilds it from the LogStore and SnapshotStore, which is why a runtime transition that leaves it stale is repaired only by restart.
after.recovery: Recomputed at construction; no handler is required to re-derive it at runtime, so each runtime transition that changes the durable log must keep it consistent itself.
unknowns: Reachability of the installSnapshot case from a legal leader history remains open: the confirmed witness needs a follower whose watermark index exceeds the leader's snapshot index (check 58ebdb2f92184614b01ecfab56fe2bc9).

After the confirmed truncation-failure case the leader's own recovery path was not exercised: whether nextIndex walks down to a resynchronizing point or the follower is left unrepaired short of a restart is still open (check 25473e1b731e4c2692e47975fef6d3a0).
